frameworks.name: Theory of Constraints for Business Growth
frameworks.definition: A business grows until it hits its constraint, then stops; entrepreneurs must identify and focus on the binding constraint rather than working on preferred tasks.

frameworks.name: Three-Path Framework for Capturing Value
frameworks.definition: When you have a high-leverage capability, choose between: partnering with a larger business, buying the business yourself, or licensing your capability to others.

frameworks.name: Building for Scale Foundation Decision
frameworks.definition: The foundation built for a $10M business differs from one for $100M; attempting to scale a 10-story foundation to 100 stories fails.

claims.text: A business grows up to its constraint and grows no longer. Most entrepreneurs work on what they enjoy rather than what the business needs because they haven't identified the correct constraint.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When the constraint is identified, effort focused on that single lever produces disproportionate impact compared to improvements elsewhere.

claims.text: In a three-step sales process where 50% convert step 1, 5% convert step 2, and 50% convert step 3, improving the bottleneck (step 2 from 5% to 15%) triples the business output, whereas improving the others by 10% each only incrementally improves by 20%.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: conversion impact of incremental improvement by step

claims.text: An appointment-setting business whose customers are low-quality (low revenue, short tenure, insufficient skills) should niche down to serve only the most valuable customer type rather than improve overall quality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Focusing on high-value customers creates a scalable economic engine because better customers refer, stay longer, and have higher budget.

claims.text: An appointment-setting business that serves $50M-$100M revenue companies with its outbound teams can build a repeatable system: six months of recruiting 50 outbound reps monthly creates 300 total reps generating revenue, with the founder owning a slice of all output.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Repeatable team hiring creates compounding headcount ownership; founder shifts from rolling the boulder each month to owning leverage on accumulated output.

numbers.axis: team scaling timeline (months) and total rep accumulation

claims.text: An HVAC marketing agency with 50 local clients that generates leads across 50 markets possesses the marketing capability equivalent to a $50M-$100M HVAC service business; the constraint is ownership, not capability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Proven lead generation and pipeline filling
claims.mechanism: The ability to fill 50 local service pipelines via marketing implies mastery of the underlying business; the agency owner captures only the service fee while clients capture the margin.
bounded_by: Does not apply to single-client or small-footprint agencies

claims.text: An HVAC marketing agency should consider learning the HVAC business, partnering with a skilled HVAC operator, or acquiring an HVAC service business and applying proven marketing to scale it; the fastest path to $10M is often the opposite path from $10M to $100M.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Marketing agency with proven category expertise
Desire to scale beyond $5M service revenue
claims.mechanism: Building a 10-story foundation differs from a 100-story foundation; attempting to scale the 10-story foundation to 100 stories fails. A half-step backward (acquiring the service business) enables 20 steps forward.
bounded_by: Does not apply if founder prefers remaining a pure service provider

claims.text: Large creators with 30M-40M+ subscribers and 97/100 media quality who want to make more money are constrained not by media capability (97/100) but by zero product sales, customer success, and sales infrastructure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: No owned products or sales infrastructure
claims.mechanism: Monetization through sponsorships and ad revenue is the least efficient model; purchasers make arbitrage on the creator's reach. The real constraint is building products and sales, not improving media from 97 to 99 quality.

numbers.axis: capability quality rating and monetization efficiency ranking

claims.text: A 100M+-impression-per-month creator (100M views when dormant) that monetizes purely via sponsorship and ad revenue is operating at least a $100M+ revenue opportunity in underlying business value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: High-volume audience reach implies ability to drive customer acquisition at scale; the revenue generated by sponsors is a fraction of the total economic value the creator could capture.

numbers.axis: monthly impressions and implied business scale

claims.text: A high-reach creator can negotiate equity in an advertiser's business (e.g., 10% of a $100M company) and focus effort to scale it to $200M-$300M, generating more value than monthly sponsorship payments.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Advertiser willing to grant equity for promotion focus
claims.mechanism: Ownership of upside scales with creator effort; directing 100M monthly impressions to a business can multiply its value 2-3x.

numbers.axis: equity ownership and business value multiplication

bounded_by: Requires willingness to reduce creative output

claims.text: A creator can identify the highest-paying advertiser category, acquire or clone a competitor in that category, and apply their audience to scale it; this approach captures full ownership and margin versus middleman sponsorship fees.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Ability to identify repeating advertiser patterns
claims.mechanism: The creator replicates what already works (based on advertiser spend patterns) rather than inventing, then combines it with audience reach to scale faster than competitors.
bounded_by: Requires business execution capability beyond content creation

claims.text: A creator can hire top executives from successful companies in a category (e.g., co-founders from a $100M software company), grant them 30% ownership stake each, and concentrate 70% to the creator; this recruits execution without dilution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Creator with capital to offer equity stakes
Target executives with prior category wins
claims.mechanism: Ownership stake attracts A-talent without requiring founder to execute the business operationally; three best executives can build three business lines in parallel.

numbers.axis: equity distribution and talent acquisition speed

bounded_by: Requires founder willingness to delegate control

claims.text: A high-reach creator can position as a creative shop producing viral ads for advertisers; this shifts from creator-as-audience-rental to creative-agency model where ad spend can scale beyond the creator's audience reach.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Creator with proven viral content track record
claims.mechanism: A viral TikTok or YouTube short proven with creator's audience can scale to 100M+ reach via paid media if underlying conversion is proven; ad spend has no limit on reach.

numbers.axis: audience reach multiplication through paid scaling

bounded_by: Requires proven conversion economics on ad spend

claims.text: The problem-solving framework for business scaling is: (1) what problem are we trying to solve, (2) over what time horizon, (3) which problem do we prefer solving or feel equipped to solve, (4) choose the path that aligns with available skills and resources.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Framing the problem explicitly in terms of solvability makes the growth path controllable and reduces the risk of pursuing wrong-direction scaling.

claims.text: Acquisition.com scales portfolio companies by recruiting A-talent with prior success (those who have already done the work); this recruitment capability determines which path (partnership, acquisition, licensing) the firm chooses for captured value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Recruiting proven talent in-house is faster and more controlled than building capability from scratch; this comparative advantage determines capital deployment strategy.

claims.text: The size of the slice of the pie matters more than the shape; owning 12.5% of a $1B company (IPO founder average) generates more value than owning 80% of a $10M company.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Enabling others to make money compounds returns more than controlling the majority of a smaller pie; IPO founders own 12.5% on average because scaling requires multiple stakeholders.

numbers.axis: ownership percentage vs total value generated

examples.text: An appointment-setting business owner served 50+ client companies with varying quality. Upon analysis, one client type consistently generated the most revenue. The business could specialize exclusively on that avatar, or partner with a larger business serving that market. If operating independently and building 50 outbound reps monthly for six months, the business would own a compounding slice of 300+ total reps' revenue.

An HVAC marketing agency running campaigns across 50 local markets for 50 different HVAC service companies demonstrated the marketing capability equivalent to a $50M-$100M HVAC service business. The owner could learn the HVAC business operationally, partner with an HVAC operator, or acquire a small HVAC service and apply proven marketing to scale it 5-10x.

A large influencer with 30M-40M subscribers across platforms, generating 100M monthly views even when dormant, focused effort on improving media quality (97 to 99 out of 100). The real constraint was zero product infrastructure, zero sales capability, and zero customer success. The influencer could license or acquire a competitor in the highest-paying advertiser category, grant equity to three top executives from successful category companies, and scale the business to $200M-$300M in value.

practices.text: When facing a scaling problem, first identify the true constraint via Theory of Constraints; improve the bottleneck lever rather than working on preferred activities.
Niche down your service delivery to serve only the highest-value customer type instead of attempting to improve overall quality across all segments.
Choose the capital deployment path (partnership, acquisition, or licensing) based on your greatest comparative advantage and available resources.
When scaling from $10M to $100M, accept that you may need to take a half-step backward (e.g., shift business model) to enable 20 steps forward.
For high-reach creators, position as a viral-creative shop producing ads for paid media amplification rather than renting audience for direct sponsorships.
Identify the highest-paying advertiser category via pattern analysis, then acquire or clone a competitor in that space and apply audience reach to scale.
